title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
description: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC MonitoringFighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the f
body: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC MonitoringFighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition."The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping"."It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday. And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday."I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV."I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month. If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

schema.headline: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire

title: Indian tourist killed after helicopters collide near Everest base camp
description: An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed t
body: An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man  killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said. It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.

schema.headline: Indian tourist killed after helicopters collide near Everest base camp

title: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
description: The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.The officials describe
body: The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft. Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran."One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".Meanwhile, the Associated Press cited two regional officials as saying that, during a weekend phone call, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran following the midterms.On Tuesday, Iran's chief negotiator with the US, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, stated: "The ball is now in America's court to prevent war.""Just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised speech.It was not immediately clear what Ghalibaf was referring to, but Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Irna on Monday that "very intensive" talks to try to end the war were under way with the US via Qatari and Pakistani mediators. Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed."Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process... We are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," Majed al-Ansari told reporters in Doha.Last week, Iranian negotiators discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions. They reportedly include lifting a naval blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

schema.headline: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections

title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
description: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabiliti
body: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure."There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible."I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility."The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace."Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said."Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security."Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.  Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

schema.headline: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

title: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
description: Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focu
body: Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday.The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion"  of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes."Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

schema.headline: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack

title: Florida plane crash investigators say jet may have broken apart before impact as family named
description: Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.The Learj
body: Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.The Learjet 60 had been bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old co-pilot, were among those who died on Sunday.The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on the road in Palm Beach.The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time (17:50 GMT)."The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, had become partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area."We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said. "We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was onboard at the time of the crash and whether it can be recovered.Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before it crashed.In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and nanny Anita Maria Cetina. The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.Nathalia Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the crash.Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."Filgueiras had spoken of her pride at receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school in an interview with a local affiliate of CBS News in 2023."I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes but I can't drive a car - I mean, I can, but a lot of people think it's funny."A spokesperson for East Coast Jets, where pilot Jeff Gregory used to work, said: "We are deeply saddened to learn that Capt Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach."He was married with two children, US media report.

schema.headline: Florida plane crash investigators say jet may have broken apart before impact as family named

title: Rubio urges Venezuela to release remaining political prisoners
description: The US has urged Venezuela to release the remaining political prisoners being held in the South American country.More than 1,000 political prisoners h
body: The US has urged Venezuela to release the remaining political prisoners being held in the South American country.More than 1,000 political prisoners have been freed since US forces seized Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in a military raid on Caracas on 3 January and took him to New York, where he faces trial on drug-trafficking and torture charges. But Venezuelan prisoners' rights group Foro Penal says 322 people remain in detention.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Venezuelan counterpart, Oliver Blanco, on Monday where he called for their release and discussed reforms aimed at laying the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections, the US state department said.The release of political prisoners has long been a demand made by Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.Machado, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025, returned to Venezuela on 25 October after living in exile for almost a year. One of her first meetings was with relatives of political detainees.Many of those in detention were arrested in the aftermath of the 2024 presidential election.The National Electoral Council (CNE) - which is dominated by government loyalists - declared the incumbent, Nicolás Maduro, the winner of the election even though copies of the voting tallies collected by the opposition and verified by independent media suggested that the opposition candidate had won.The Carter Center, which had sent independent observers to Venezuela, also said that the election "could not be considered democratic".A UN fact-finding mission found, external that in the months that followed, the Venezuelan government orchestrated "a harsh repression against persons perceived as political opponents or simply because they express dissent or critical views against the authorities".After US forces seized Maduro, his loyal vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim president.While Rodríguez has the backing of the Trump administration, opposition parties within Venezuela have been expressing impatience with the slow pace of reforms.In Monday's statement, the US state department stressed that it remained committed to US President Donald Trump's three-phase plan, consisting of "stabilisation, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition".A week ago, Rubio had told journalists that Venezuela's "election infrastructure" had to be replaced in order for fresh elections to be valid."Not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years; it needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established," he insisted.Days later, Rodríguez told Venezuelans in a televised address that "there will be elections" under a "renewed" electoral authority.However, she did not give a timeline for when the election could be held. Opposition leader Machado, on the other hand, has been pushing for elections to be held in 2027.At one point she suggested 24 July 2027 - the anniversary of the birth of independence hero Simón Bolivar - but she has since returned to calling for a vote at some point in the next year.

schema.headline: Rubio urges Venezuela to release remaining political prisoners

title: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
description: The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores,
body: The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives.""These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.

schema.headline: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries

title: Russian bombing kills 31 people at humanitarian aid centre in Ukraine, Kyiv sayss
description: At least 31 people have been killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre in Zaporizhia, the Ukrainian regional head has said, describing
body: At least 31 people have been killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre in Zaporizhia, the Ukrainian regional head has said, describing it as one of the deadliest attacks there since the start of the full-scale invasion.Mykhailo Semikin said at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in southern Ukraine on Monday and the aid centre collapsed from a "direct hit"."They had come for help - not to a military facility, not to a frontline position, but to a place where they were supposed to receive support," he wrote on Telegram.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the attack "utterly horrific" and said there were still people "under the rubble".Zelensky posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack and rescuers searching for survivors.However, officials say teams have at times been forced to halt their search because of Russian drone attacks in the area.Zelensky said after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.The Russian military has not publicly commented.

schema.headline: Russian bombing kills 31 people at humanitarian aid centre in Ukraine, Kyiv sayss

title: Major test for Australia's social media ban begins in High Court
description: Australia's rush to put in place a landmark social media ban for children led to "ill thought out" reforms which have robbed them of their right to fr
body: Australia's rush to put in place a landmark social media ban for children led to "ill thought out" reforms which have robbed them of their right to free communication, the country's top court has been told.In a major test for the world-leading policy, online forum Reddit and a digital rights group argued at a hearing on Tuesday that the law should be struck down as it is unconstitutional.Introduced last December, the ban is among a number of online safety reforms the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years.Supporters say it protects children from harmful content, but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.Speaking outside the High Court in Canberra, Communications Minister Anika Wells said the question of what society is willing to accept from tech platforms is "the most compelling policy question of our time"."We are here to defend a fundamental tenet of Australian democracy, which is an Australian's right, and particularly an Australian child's right, to be free from harm," Wells said."We seek to defend that from sustained ideological attack."The constitutional challenge was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is led by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick, who told reporters outside the court the policy amounted to "censorship".Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs. The teens have yet to publicly state their reasons for doing so.But Jones told media outside the court that children deserved to have their voices heard."If the children aren't collaborating and sharing their own views, then they're just spectators in their own world," he said, according to Nine newspapers.Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.The company said it shared Australia's goal of protecting young people online "but there are better and more effective ways" than a ban."As we challenge this law in court, we'll continue to comply with it and advocate for more effective youth safety measures," said Reddit's chief communications officer Adam Collins.Inside the courtroom, the company's lawyer Perry Herzfeld argued the law breached the freedom of political expression implied in Australia's constitution by restricting children from the most important means of communication in the modern world.He said the ban was "ill thought out" and contradicted the advice of Australia's online safety tsar, and was rushed through without true public consultation - pointing out they had only 24 hours to make submissions about the law.Meanwhile government lawyer Joanna Davidson SC, began outlining for the full bench of the High Court why the government believed social media harmed children. She will continue presenting her case on Wednesday.Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined. The eSafety Commissioner - the body tasked with enforcing the ban - has launched several investigations into alleged non-compliance by Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube.WhatsApp and online gaming sites like Roblox and Discord were not included in the ban, nor were educational platforms like YouTube Kids and Google Classroom.In the first few days of the ban, Meta - which owns three of the banned platforms - said it had closed about half a million accounts.Some children said they were booted off their accounts in the days before and when the ban started - but many have said they were able to easily circumvent the age checks which included uploading credit card details, photo IDs or a selfie.

schema.headline: Major test for Australia's social media ban begins in High Court

title: Agoa: Donald Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
description: US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January
body: US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.For South Africa, the US pointed to corruption.In a letter to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Trump said Pretoria's actions on international security and its relations and cooperation with governments of concern to Washington risked undermining US national security and foreign policy interests.He also accused South Africa of maintaining significant barriers to American trade and investment, including restrictions affecting agricultural market access, regulatory requirements, investment protections and intellectual property."The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the decision as "unfortunate", saying Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade negotiations between the two countries, which began in 2025."We will continue to accelerate the diversification of South Africa's export markets to protect jobs," Tau said.South Africa has also sought to put the potential impact of losing Agoa benefits into perspective, arguing that the country's broader trade relationship with the US extends well beyond the programme.Government figures show that about 89% of South African exports to the US entered under ordinary World Trade Organization most-favoured-nation terms in 2025, while around 10% benefited from Agoa, down from 28% in 2024."The value of South African exports under the programme fell to about $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in 2025, from $4bn the previous year," Tau said.Bilateral trade between the two countries reached $28.8bn in 2025, while more than 600 American companies operate in South Africa, supporting about 134,600 jobs.Pretoria says the two economies have complementary trade interests. South Africa supplies 12 of the 50 minerals considered critical by the US, as well as 70% of American isotopes used, among other things, in cancer treatment.South African manufacturers also use American inputs in products exported to the US under Agoa, including vehicles and boats.Oxford Economics senior economist Jee-A van der Linde said Washington's move will put further pressure on South Africa's manufacturing sector, warning that affected exports may be difficult to redirect to other markets."This decision comes as global trade flows remained disrupted and South Africa faces growing competition from cheap Chinese imports, particularly in the automotive industry," he said.However, he noted that South Africa had previously managed to redirect some tariff-affected exports to markets including Europe and China.US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa. "This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.Last year, Trump accused South Africa of persecuting its white minority and launched a programme for white Afrikaners to get asylum in the US.Trump also repeated widely discredited claims of a genocide of South Africa's white population.In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights. The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training. Rwanda has denied backing the M23 despite overwhelming evidence.Rwanda saw its exports to the US rise to $43.3 million in 2025, up from $13.1 million in 2024, according to US import data.Alexander Venter, an Oxford Economics economist, said Washington accounted for about 2% of Rwanda's merchandise exports in 2025, with only around 4% of its exports to the US benefiting from Agoa preferences.Neighbouring African countries and Asian markets continued to dominate Rwanda's trade, Venter added.

schema.headline: Agoa: Donald Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal

title: Elon Musk pumps $446m into US midterms, as campaign spending set to 'shatter' records
description: The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record
body: The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle."Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.

schema.headline: Elon Musk pumps $446m into US midterms, as campaign spending set to 'shatter' records

title: Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?
description: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentThe Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midt
body: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentThe Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.But are the polls accurate?Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate."Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate. It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeatPolling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.Figure caption, Voter voices: What issues matter most to Americans?There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science."I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."Do you have questions about the US midterms? Click here or use the form below.Get in touchWhat questions do you have?Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

title: Western Sahara: Morocco celebrates end of the UN mission Minurso
description: Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds alon
body: Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory. The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI."The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR). But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.  In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel. France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation. Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps."Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online. Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."Polisario has not said what it will do next.Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

schema.headline: Western Sahara: Morocco celebrates end of the UN mission Minurso

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
description: Image source, Getty ImagesBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesThe US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administrati
body: Image source, Getty ImagesBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesThe US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count. The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state. Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate. The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term. The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction. "The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots. California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots.In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots.California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies.They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible. Figure caption, What are Americans voting for this election?The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare.President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states.Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration.The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch". With additional reporting by the BBC's David Willis

schema.headline: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
